lines.text: Communication in English extends far beyond simply 'saying' and 'telling'. The language offers dozens of verbs that specify how something is communicated — the volume, emotion, intention, and context behind every utterance. Volume verbs range from whisper (speak very softly) and murmur (speak quietly and indistinctly) to shout (speak loudly), yell (shout with emotion), scream (cry out in fear or excitement), and bellow (shout in a deep, powerful voice). Emotional speech verbs include grumble (complain quietly), moan (express dissatisfaction), sob (speak while crying), stammer and stutter (speak with involuntary repetition), and snap (speak sharply in irritation). Persuasion and argument verbs encompass argue (exchange opposing views), debate (discuss formally), negotiate (discuss to reach agreement), persuade (convince someone), urge (strongly encourage), and insist (demand firmly). Information-sharing verbs distinguish between announce (declare publicly), reveal (make known something hidden), confess (admit something embarrassing or wrong), mention (refer to briefly), and hint (suggest indirectly). Professional communication uses verbs like brief (give concise information), summarise (give the main points), elaborate (explain in more detail), clarify (make clearer), and specify (state precisely). Mastering these verbs transforms reporting and storytelling, allowing speakers to show rather than tell how people communicate.

lines.text: British communication is famously indirect. 'That's an interesting idea' often means 'I disagree'. 'With the greatest respect...' usually precedes strong criticism. 'I'll bear that in mind' often means 'I'll ignore that'. This indirectness is a skill, not evasiveness.
lines.name: British communication is famously indirect. 'That's an interesting idea' often means 'I disagree'. 'With the greatest respect...' usually precedes strong criticism. 'I'll bear that in mind' often means 'I'll ignore that'. This indirectness is a skill, not evasiveness.

lines.text: Academic English uses precise reporting verbs: 'The author argues/claims/maintains/asserts/contends/suggests/proposes/implies'. Each carries different weight — 'claims' implies doubt, 'demonstrates' implies proof, 'suggests' implies possibility.

lines.text: British email etiquette has its own verb conventions: 'I'm writing to enquire about...' (formal), 'Just dropping you a line about...' (informal), 'Please don't hesitate to contact me' (closing). Americans tend to be more direct in emails.

lines.text: English has many words for gossip: 'rumour', 'hearsay', 'word on the street', 'grapevine' ('I heard it through the grapevine'). Gossip verbs: 'spread rumours', 'badmouth', 'talk behind someone's back', 'dish the dirt', 'spill the tea' (modern slang).

lines.text: In British education, debating is a valued skill. Key phrases: 'I'd like to put forward the argument that...', 'With respect, I disagree because...', 'That's a fair point, however...'. The ability to disagree politely while arguing firmly is considered an essential communication skill.

lines.text: 'Say' doesn't take an indirect object before 'to'. Use 'tell + person + to do something' or 'say + that clause'. Never 'say me/him/her'.

lines.text: 'Discuss' is transitive — it takes a direct object, no 'about'. Similarly: 'mention the issue' (not 'mention about').

lines.text: 'Tell' requires a person: 'She told me/us/them that...'. 'Say' doesn't need one: 'She said that...'. Confusing these is a very common error.
